subject: AI & Agents
title: Recurrent Neural Networks: Memory for Sequences
description: A short lesson to help you apply Recurrent Neural Networks: Memory for Sequences.

hook.text: Regular networks forget everything between inputs. Recurrent networks remember — they have loops.

buildup.text: RNNs pass information from one step to the next, maintaining a hidden state like short-term memory.

discovery.text: This makes them natural for sequences — text, speech, music, stock prices over time.

twist.text: Vanilla RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients — they forget long-ago context. LSTMs fixed this.

climax.text: Transformers eventually replaced RNNs for most tasks, but the concept of memory in networks endures.

punchline.text: To understand a sentence, remember its start. Networks learned that.

quiz.question: What problem do recurrent neural networks solve?
options: Processing sequential data by maintaining memory between steps

details.summary: RNNs and their variants LSTM and GRU maintain structured memory cells that selectively remember or forget information across long sequences. This gating mechanism solved the vanishing gradient problem.
details.whyItMatters: LSTM and GRU networks enabled AI to process long sequences like paragraphs and time series. Their gating innovations paved the way for the attention mechanisms used in modern Transformers.
takeaways: LSTM and GRU add gates that control memory retention and forgetting
Gates solve the vanishing gradient problem over long sequences
These innovations laid groundwork for modern attention mechanisms

faq.question: What are LSTM gates and what do they do?
faq.answer: LSTM has three gates: forget, input, and output. The forget gate discards irrelevant past information. The input gate adds new relevant information. The output gate controls what gets passed forward as the hidden state.

faq.question: Are LSTMs still relevant with Transformers dominating?
faq.answer: LSTMs are less common for large-scale tasks but remain useful where compute is limited, sequences are very long, or real-time processing requires simple architectures, such as edge devices and simple time series.
